tldr: The authors propose Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), an approach that lets users specify execution qualities like speed and smoothness at inference time. By combining online rollouts prompted with top-quality labels and an iterative hindsight relabeling loop, it achieves high success rates while significantly surpassing the quality of the initial demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed method QCP and Iterative Hindsight Relabeling. As shown on the left, quality labels (tokens) can be specified at inference time to adjust robot behaviors. Through the loop on the right, the policy collects top-quality rollouts and repeatedly relabels them, evolving beyond the initial demonstrations toward higher-quality execution.
overview:
In robot learning, imitation learning using Behavior Cloning (BC) on successful demonstration trajectories is the standard approach. However, conventional BC treats all successful demonstrations equally. This averages out various execution styles in the data—such as fast versus slow, or smooth versus jerky—preventing users from controlling behavioral characteristics to fit deployment needs. For instance, throughput speed is paramount for conveyor operations, whereas horizontal stability is critical when carrying wine glasses.

To address this, the authors propose Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), which conditions the policy on discretized quality labels. Furthermore, to break through the quality ceiling of offline initial demonstrations, they introduce an "Iterative Hindsight Relabeling" loop. In this setup, the policy performs autonomous rollouts conditioned on the highest-quality label, relabels successful trajectories in hindsight based on their measured quality, adds them to the dataset, and retrains the policy.

Evaluated on simulators (Robomimic, RoboEval) and real-world manipulation tasks (Franka Research 3), QCP substantially improved motion quality while boosting task success rates, far exceeding the upper bound of the initial demonstrations. Real-robot experiments also demonstrated direct practical utility in physical deployments, such as increasing throughput on conveyor operations (from 8.2 to 13.0 items/min) and reducing tray tilt when transporting wine (from 0.0660 to 0.0482 rad).
contributions: Proposal of QCP, a Flow Matching-based policy capable of controlling single and multiple execution qualities (e.g., speed, smoothness, path length) at inference time.

Development of an autonomous loop that expands the quality range beyond initial demonstrations by collecting rollouts under the highest-quality label, relabeling them in hindsight using measured quality, and retraining.
Demonstration that QCP resolves the trade-off between task success rate and motion quality compared to reinforcement learning (RL) and data-filtering BC baselines, simultaneously improving both.
Validation on real-world Franka arms and a VLA model ($\pi_{0.5}$), proving practical efficacy through increased conveyor throughput and stabilized wine transport.

sections.heading: Controlling not just success, but "how" the robot moves
sections.summary: Conventional imitation learning in robotics focuses only on task completion and cannot control execution quality. This work proposes QCP to specify quality at inference time, alongside an iterative relabeling loop that acquires behaviors exceeding the demonstrations through online collection.
sections.details:
Recent advances in robot foundation models have dramatically improved generalization capabilities, yet most rely on Behavior Cloning (BC) over successful demonstrations. Because BC treats every successful trajectory equally, it merely reproduces the mixture of various execution styles contained in the data. Consequently, it cannot handle practical deployment requirements, such as "move faster right now" or "handle this gently because it is fragile."

Existing style-control methods do exist, but because they rely on static demonstration datasets, they cannot surpass the quality ceiling present in those demonstrations. Acquiring top-tier behaviors, such as maximum speed or ideal smoothness, requires pushing performance beyond the support of the initial demonstrations.

This is where the proposed method comes in. The authors introduce QCP, which converts quality scores measured by rule-based functions into discrete quantile bins (quality labels) and feeds them as conditioning inputs to the policy. Furthermore, by pairing this with "Iterative Hindsight Relabeling"—which rolls out with the top-quality label, recomputes actual measured scores of successful trajectories, updates the dataset, and retrains—the policy autonomously evolves beyond the demonstrations without needing any additional human annotations.

sections.heading: At the intersection of style control and online quality improvement
sections.summary: Learning behavioral styles often suffers from a trade-off against task success rate, and online preference learning incurs high human annotation burdens. This work overcomes both challenges using automated scoring and relabeling.
sections.details:
### Policy Learning with Quality Control
Prior work has explored controlling motion styles using trajectory representations or explicit labels. However, strictly adhering to a designated style often creates tension with task success, leading to a performance trade-off. While prior studies like SORL and SCIQL attempted to address this with advantage-weighted reinforcement learning, tuning remains difficult. QCP achieves simultaneous improvements in both success rate and quality by combining quality-label conditioning with iterative relabeling.

### Online Improvement of Motion Quality
Some approaches learn reward models from human feedback to update policies (e.g., Freeform Preference Learning), but they require burdensome human comparison annotations at every iteration. Meanwhile, in the language model domain, methods like Quark have shown strong results by sampling with high-reward tokens, relabeling outputs by quantiles, and retraining. QCP adapts this concept to robot motion quality control. By leveraging rule-based scoring functions, it expands the controllable quality range without requiring extra human labeling.

sections.heading: QCP architecture and the iterative hindsight relabeling mechanism
sections.summary: Quality scores are discretized into equal-frequency bins to condition a Flow Matching policy. Successful trajectories collected under the top-quality label are relabeled with their measured values, updating the whole dataset to re-initialize and retrain the model.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Quality-Controllable Policy
- **Quality Scores and Discretization**: For a successful trajectory $\tau$, a rule-based function $m(\tau)$ is defined to measure the execution quality of interest (e.g., the reciprocal of execution steps $1/T$ as a speed metric). This score is partitioned into $B$ equal-frequency bins (the paper primarily uses $B=4$ quartiles), assigning a discrete label $q(\tau) \in \{0, \ldots, B-1\}$ to each trajectory.
- **Policy Training**: The policy $\pi_\theta$ adopts the widely used Flow Matching framework. It takes the observation history $h_t$ over the past $L$ steps and the quality label $q$ as inputs to predict future action chunks $A_t$. When trained from scratch, the label is vectorized via an embedding layer and concatenated with inputs. For Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, it is inserted into the language prompt as text, such as "quality level: 3".
- **Inference-Time Control**: At test time, simply specifying a target bin $q^\star$ allows the policy to generate actions via numerical integration from noise, executing the task at the desired quality level.

### 3.2 Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
To surpass the quality of the initial demonstrations, the authors repeat the following loop:
1. Rollouts are collected from the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$ by specifying the highest-quality bin $q^\star = B-1$.
2. Only successful trajectories are kept. Since actual scores vary even when requesting the highest quality, trajectories are **relabeled in hindsight based on their measured scores $m(\tau)$**.
3. These trajectories are added to the dataset, and bin boundaries are recomputed across the score distribution of all accumulated trajectories. This progressively raises the quality bar represented by the top bin.
4. The next policy $\pi_{\theta_{k+1}}$ is trained. As a crucial design choice, rather than fine-tuning from the previous policy checkpoint, **the weights are re-initialized and trained from scratch each time**. Because changing bin boundaries shifts the mapping between labels and behaviors, resetting the previous associations proves more effective.

sections.heading: Quality control and performance gains verified in simulation and the real world
sections.summary: In Robomimic and RoboEval, QCP simultaneously improved success rate and quality, outperforming existing RL baselines. Real Franka arm experiments also confirmed substantial gains in throughput and transport stability.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Robomimic (Square, Transport) and RoboEval (Pack Box, Pick Book, etc.) were used as simulation environments. Baselines included $\text{BC}_{\text{acc}}$ (accumulating successful trajectories), $\text{BC}_{\text{filter}}$ (training only on top-scoring data), offline RL methods (SORL, SCIQL), and online RL methods for Flow Matching (DSRL, EXPO). Evaluation metrics were task success rates and respective quality measures (speed, jerk, joint travel distance, etc.).

### 4.2 Quality and Success Rate Improvements Across Iterations
$\text{BC}_{\text{filter}}$ and SORL suffered in success rate because filtering out data reduced the total dataset size. Online RL struggled to optimize quality rewards effectively. In contrast, QCP steadily improved both success rate and motion quality across iterations (outperforming RL baselines in Table 1) because it retains lower-quality trajectories to learn task completion while differentiating them via labels.

### 4.3 Quality Controllability and Range Expansion
Even when trained only on initial demonstrations, clear variations in speed and smoothness were observed depending on the specified bin ($q=0$ to $3$). With repeated iterations, the distributions of smoothness and joint travel distance pushed far beyond the range of the initial demonstrations, achieving a large distribution shift exceeding 1.5 in normalized Wasserstein distance.

### 4.4 Multi-Attribute Joint Control
QCP successfully demonstrated simultaneous two-attribute control (e.g., "high speed and low lift" or "low speed and high lift") and joint optimization of up to six attributes in RoboEval. This highlights its flexibility to achieve multi-attribute improvements comparable to single-attribute tuning.

### 4.5 Real-World Robot Experiments
Two physical manipulation tasks were tested using a Franka Research 3 arm and the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA model.
- **Wine Serving (Stability Focus)**: A challenging task where keeping the tray horizontal is difficult, yielding only a 13.1% success rate under human teleoperation. When prompting QCP with the highest stability bin, the average tray tilt decreased by 27.0% from 0.0660 rad (BC) to 0.0482 rad, and the success rate increased from 30.7% to 42.0%.
- **Conveyor Operations (Speed Focus)**: Grasping cans moving at regular intervals. QCP boosted end-effector speed by 36.6% (from 188.6 mm/s to 257.6 mm/s) and raised throughput by 59.3% from 8.2 to 13.0 cans/min. This agility significantly surpassed even human teleoperation (173.5 mm/s).

captions.F7: Experimental results on the real Franka robot. (a) In the wine-serving task, tray tilt angle is reduced and success rate reaches 42.0%. (b) In the conveyor operation task, end-effector (EEF) speed is increased, raising throughput to 13.0 items/min. In both setups, QCP clearly outperforms standard BC and filtering baselines.

sections.heading: Why does QCP work? Detailed ablations
sections.summary: Ablations confirm that performance gains stem from the relabeling loop rather than mere extensive sampling. Furthermore, discrete labels like quartiles provide much more stable training than continuous scores.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Effect on Rollout Distribution
The authors investigated whether iterative quality improvement was simply an artifact of "sampling many times under the top bin until an unusually good trajectory appeared." Comparing 1,800 rollouts sampled from the initial policy (iteration 0) against training iteratively with 300 rollouts per loop revealed that the static policy never generated the ultra-smooth behaviors found in later iterations. This confirms that the relabeling and retraining loop genuinely pushes the policy's execution envelope.

### 5.2 Continuous Scores vs. Discretized Quality Labels
Conditioning on raw continuous scores was compared against binning into discrete labels. When using four discrete bins, roughly 25% of the training data shares the top label, providing a stable supervisory signal. Experiments showed that continuous conditioning lagged in both speed and success rate. Conversely, partitioning into too many bins (8, 16, or 32) caused the data volume in the top bin to shrink excessively, precipitating a steep drop in success rate (down to 28.1% with 32 bins). A 4-bin (quartile) discrete label proved the most robust and high-performing setup.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: QCP unifies inference-time control over execution quality and out-of-demonstration performance gains using discrete quality labels and iterative relabeling. It is a practical, general framework for diverse attributes measurable by rule-based functions.
sections.details:
This paper presented QCP, a robot policy that enables flexible inference-time control over single or multiple motion attributes by conditioning on discretized quality labels. Through an "Iterative Hindsight Relabeling" loop requiring zero additional human annotations, the method expands the policy's quality envelope well beyond the limits of initial demonstrations via online rollouts.

Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world environments demonstrated that execution speed, smoothness, and stability can be dramatically improved without compromising task completion rates. This offers a highly practical and capable approach for dictating exactly "how the robot should behave" in physical deployments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Metric definitions and segment-level relabeling validation
sections.summary: Presents exact mathematical formulations for quality metrics and evaluates why trajectory-level labeling outperforms local segment-level labeling.
sections.details:
### Detailed Quality Score Definitions
- **Execution Speed**: Number of steps to completion $T$ (or its reciprocal $1/T$); measured as end-effector speed (mm/s) on the real robot.
- **Action Smoothness**: Sum of squared differences between consecutive actions normalized by action magnitude (action jerk). Lower values indicate smoother motions.
- **Real-World Wine Transport Stability**: End-effector tilt angle $\bar{\theta}$ (rad) relative to the vertical axis. Lower values correspond to keeping the tray more horizontal.

### Trajectory-Level vs. Segment-Level Labeling
The authors compared assigning a single label to the entire trajectory against labeling local segments of a few steps (Appendix G).
Segment-level scores proved heavily dependent on the task phase (e.g., approach phase versus insertion phase), meaning optimizing local scores did not translate into full task completion. Consequently, QCP's design of assigning labels to the full trajectory achieved the highest performance in both success rate and overall quality.

takeaways: Conditioning the policy on discrete quality labels (e.g., speed, smoothness) alongside binary task success enables knob-like adjustment of behavioral traits at inference time.
Relabeling data collected under the highest-quality label in hindsight with actual measured values autonomously pushes policy quality beyond the initial demonstrations.
Filtering datasets to only top percentiles harms task success rates by reducing diversity, whereas retaining all data with quality labels preserves and improves success while raising quality.
Discretizing scores into a moderate number of equal-frequency bins (around 4 quartiles) offers far more stable training support than using continuous raw scores.
limitations: Applicability is restricted to attributes for which humans can explicitly design rule-based quality score functions (e.g., steps, jerk, tilt).
Because bin boundaries shift every iteration, the policy must be retrained from scratch (or from a pretrained checkpoint), incurring moderate computational overhead.
Achieving finer-grained quality control at the segment level remains challenging due to interference between local quality improvements and overall task progress.
